meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Did You Lose the Keys Here? No, But the Light Is Much Better Here'?
meta.ogDescription: The joke behind the “streetlight effect”. Earliest known printing: a Boston paper, May 1924 — and the lost object was a $2 bill, not keys.

answer.label: Not Evan Esar — an anonymous newspaper joke from 1924
answer.authorDates: First in print 24 May 1924 · no author was ever named
answer.sourceLine: Nobody owns this joke. Quote Investigator’s earliest located instance ↗ is an unsigned item in the Boston Herald of 24 May 1924 — and the man was hunting a $2 bill, not keys. Evan Esar, the quotation anthologist whose name is attached to it, printed a version in Esar’s Joke Dictionary in 1945, twenty-one years later; he was collecting it, not writing it. Two further points of honesty: QI says earlier instances are likely still to be found, and the exact two-line exchange at the top of this page is QI’s own article title, not words transcribed from any period source.

source.heading: The earliest known printing: Boston, May 1924

docMeta.dd: 24 May 1924, quote page 2, column 1 (located by Quote Investigator via GenealogyBank)
None — newspaper filler, no author named
A $2 bill on Atlantic Avenue. The 1920s tellings lose money or a watch; the key only arrives in the 1950s

source.excerpt: “I lost a $2 bill down on Atlantic avenue,” said the man. “What’s that?” asked the puzzled officer. “You lost a $2 bill on Atlantic avenue? Then why are you hunting around here in Copley square?” “Because,” said the man as he turned away and continued his hunt on his hands and knees, “the light’s better up here.”
source.trailTitle: How the joke travelled, and when the keys appeared
trail: 1924 — Two instances within five months, both unsigned, in two different cities: the Boston Herald on 24 May (a $2 bill, Copley Square) and the National Labor Tribune of Pittsburgh on 2 October, under the heading “Better Light” (an Englishman, a dollar bill, Sunset Boulevard). Both located by Quote Investigator ↗. A joke appearing twice in one year in two local papers was already in circulation before either printed it.

1925–1942 — The object keeps changing and the frame keeps moving. A watch lost at 23rd Street (Kingston Daily Freeman, 21 February 1925); a dime (Bridgeport Telegram, 28 September 1927); a five-dollar bill, told by “Mr. Sniff” and “Mr. Snoop” with nobody drunk at all, in the Boy Scouts’ Boys’ Life for October 1932; a quarter, in the Mutt and Jeff comic strip of 3 June 1942; and a matchbox, in Henri-Georges Clouzot’s French film L’Assassin habite… au 21, also 1942 — the chronology QI assembled ↗.

1945 — Evan Esar’s turn, and the only reason his name is on this page. Esar’s Joke Dictionary (Harvest House, New York) carries the lamppost version on page 140, spelled to suggest slurred speech, and the lost object is a quarter — verified with scans by QI ↗. Esar was an anthologist: Esar’s Comic Dictionary (1943), 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968). Appearing in a collection of other people’s jokes is the opposite of authorship.

1954 onward — and the keys. Abraham Maslow alluded to it in Motivation and Personality (1954, p. 16) as “the famous drunk” looking for his wallet. The lost item first becomes a key in 1956, in a Canadian column quoting the geologist Frederick H. Pough on uranium prospecting, and again in a 1967 address to the American Radium Society titled “The Light Is Better Here” — both in QI’s citations ↗. The keys-and-streetlight telling that names the “streetlight effect”, or drunkard’s search principle ↗ is therefore the youngest part of a joke that is a century old.
source.excerptNote: The oldest version anyone has found, as Quote Investigator transcribes it ↗. Note what is already fixed and what is not: the policeman, the wrong street, the punchline about the light — all present. The keys are not. Neither is the drunkenness, stated outright; the man is simply “groping about” near midnight.
source.rightsNote: The exact two-line exchange displayed at the top of this page is the title of a Quote Investigator article first published on 11 April 2013, so it is modern text rather than a historical quotation, and that is what the in-copyright flag refers to. The period tellings are a different matter: the 1924 Boston Herald and National Labor Tribune items, the 1925 and 1927 newspaper versions and the 1932 Boys’ Life gag are all long out of copyright in the United States. The joke itself has no identified author, so there is no estate to clear.

author.name: Evan Esar
author.kicker: The man who got the credit
author.heading: So who was Evan Esar?
author.bio: Evan Esar spent a long career collecting and classifying other people’s jokes. His Comic Dictionary (1943) arranged comic definitions alphabetically, Esar’s Joke Dictionary followed in 1945, and 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968) became a standard desk reference — which is why his lines still turn up in crossword clues. He also wrote The Legend of Joe Miller, privately printed for the Roxburghe Club of San Francisco in 1957, a study of the eighteenth-century comedian whose name became a byword for a recycled joke. That is the irony of his appearance here: Esar was a scholar of jokes that had lost their authors, and he has now been handed one.

misattribution.heading: Four candidate origins, none of them first
misattribution.intro: Quote Investigator opened its investigation by naming the four sources people propose for this joke. Every one of them postdates the 1924 newspapers — in two cases by decades.

items.why: His Joke Dictionary (1945) does carry the joke, on page 140 — QI verified the page with scans ↗ — but twenty-one years after the Boston Herald. Esar made his name compiling other people’s wit ↗: Esar’s Comic Dictionary (1943), Humorous English (1961), 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968). A compiler’s book is evidence that a joke was already current.

A version in which Nasreddin loses a ring indoors and searches the sunlit yard appears in Classic Tales of Mulla Nasreddin — but that collection was published in 1989, as QI notes ↗, and QI adds that it is not clear when this particular tale entered the compendium. Nasreddin’s own historicity is an open question ↗, and new stories have been added to his cycle in every generation, so a Nasreddin telling cannot by itself date the joke — in either direction.

items.scope: The magazine and the comic strip
items.who: Boys’ Life (1932) and Mutt and Jeff (1942)
items.why: Both are real appearances and both are late. The Boys’ Life “Think and Grin” version of October 1932 drops the drink entirely; the Mutt and Jeff strip of 3 June 1942 has Jeff hunting a quarter under a lamppost. QI dates and transcribes both ↗ — eight and eighteen years after 1924.

items.scope: Where the credit usually goes today
items.why: Maslow’s Motivation and Personality (1954, p. 16) is how the joke entered the research-methods literature, and it is why the bias has a name. But he introduced it as “the famous drunk” — his wording, in QI’s citation ↗ — which is an author telling you he did not invent it.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is anonymous. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the earliest known documented instances are from 1924 ↗, that an earlier origin is likely, and that no creator has been identified — so the honest credit is to nobody.

context.heading: The joke that named a bias
lead: This is a rare case of a newspaper gag becoming a working concept in science. The “streetlight effect”, also called the drunkard’s search principle ↗, is the observational bias of looking for something where looking is easiest rather than where the thing is — measuring what the instrument can measure and calling that the phenomenon. Maslow put the joke into Motivation and Personality in 1954 to make exactly that point, and researchers have been reaching for it ever since.

The drift of the lost object tells you how the joke was used. In the 1920s it was money — a $2 bill, a dollar, a dime — because the audience was being invited to laugh at a drunk. By the 1950s it is a key, which is what you reach for when the point is no longer the drunk but the search: a key is small, specific, and either in the light or not. The modern telling is better engineered for the argument it now has to carry.
detailsBody: The Boston Herald item has no policeman-and-drunk framing in the modern sense. A man is “groping about” on his hands and knees near midnight in Copley Square; an officer asks what he is doing; he says he lost a $2 bill down on Atlantic Avenue; the officer asks the obvious question; the man answers that the light is better up here and goes back to searching. He is never called drunk.

Five months later the National Labor Tribune ran it with an Englishman holding onto a lamp post on Hollywood Boulevard who has lost a dollar on “Shunset boulvar” — the slurred spelling doing the work the first version left to the reader. Two unsigned tellings, two cities, one year: by 1924 this was already a joke in circulation rather than anyone’s invention.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator’s earliest located instance of the joke is an unsigned item in the Boston Herald of 24 May 1924 ("Whiting’s Column," quote page 2, column 1) in which a man searching in Copley Square says he lost a $2 bill on Atlantic Avenue "because the light’s better up here"; further instances are dated 2 October 1924 (National Labor Tribune, "Better Light"), 21 February 1925 (Kingston Daily Freeman), 28 September 1927 (Bridgeport Telegram), October 1932 (Boys’ Life, "Think and Grin", p. 36), 3 June 1942 (Mutt and Jeff), 1942 (the Clouzot film L’Assassin habite... au 21), 1945 (Esar’s Joke Dictionary, Harvest House, p. 140, verified with scans), 1954 (Maslow, Motivation and Personality, p. 16), 1956 (Lethbridge Herald, quoting geologist Frederick H. Pough), 1967 (American Radium Society president’s address, "The Light Is Better Here") and 1989 (Classic Tales of Mulla Nasreddin, p. 26). QI concludes the earliest known documented instances are from 1924, that antedating is quite likely, and names no creator.

Wikipedia states Evan Esar (1899–1995) was an American humorist who wrote Esar’s Comic Dictionary in 1943, Humorous English in 1961 and 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968, that his quotes are commonly found in crossword puzzles, and that he wrote The Legend of Joe Miller, privately printed for the Roxburghe Club of San Francisco by the Grabhorn Press in 1957.

Wikipedia’s "Streetlight effect" article states the streetlight effect, or the drunkard’s search principle, is a type of observational bias occurring when people only search for something where it is easiest to look, tells the joke in the keys-under-the-streetlight form, and notes the anecdote appears in a story of the folklore character Nasreddin.

Wikipedia states Nasreddin is a character in the folklore of Central Asia appearing in thousands of stories across dozens of languages, and that the specific date or place of his birth, and his historicity, remain an open question.
